stories.title: La liste de ma mère
stories.summary: A narrator goes shopping with their mother's illegible list, guesses wrong three times, and comes home to a meal made from the mistakes.

lines.en: Every Saturday, my mother writes a list for the shopping.
Her handwriting is really hard to read.
Nobody understands it well.

notes.note: «personne» is doing the job of the subject here — nobody — not sitting after the verb the way it does in «il n'y a personne». It still pairs with «ne» the same way «plus» and «jamais» do; the two words just wrap around «la comprend» instead of following it.

lines.en: This morning, she gave me the list and a little money.

notes.note: «m'» stands for "me" and sits right in front of «a», the helper verb. English says "gave me" with "me" after the verb; French moves it left and glues it there instead.
«un peu» already says how much — a little — so French doesn't reach for a partitive article on top of it. It drops straight to bare «de», and you'll see the same move with «beaucoup de» in a moment.
«de» runs into «argent», a word starting with a vowel, so it drops its own vowel and becomes «d'». Saying «de argent» out loud is impossible, which is exactly why the contraction exists.

lines.en: There's no more milk or bread in the house.

notes.note: «il», «y», and «a» only mean something together — there is. It's the same fixed block that names what's missing from the house before the narrator even leaves for the shop.
«plus» here doesn't mean "more" — paired with «ne», it means "not any more". The house hasn't got a little milk left, it's completely out.
«lait» would normally take «du» in front of it — some milk. Once the sentence is negative, there isn't any, so the article shrinks to bare «de». The same thing happens to «pain» a few words later.
«pain» would also take «du» on its own — some bread. Because the whole sentence stays negative, it drops to bare «de» here too, exactly the same move as «lait» just before it.

lines.en: I went to the shop on the corner of the street.

notes.note: «aller» is one of the small set of verbs — mostly about movement — that build the passé composé with «être» instead of «avoir». That's why it's «je suis allé», never «j'ai allé».

lines.en: There were a lot of people in the shop.

notes.note: Same fixed phrase as a moment ago, just in the imparfait now — «il y avait» paints the scene the narrator walked into, the crowd already there before anything else happened.
Same move as «un peu d'argent» earlier: «beaucoup» already names the amount, so «monde» gets bare «de» in front of it instead of a partitive article.

lines.en: On the list, I read "bread", "eggs" and "butter".

notes.note: «pain» is masculine, so «de» plus «le» contracts to «du» — some bread, an amount with no number attached, not one whole specific loaf.
Same idea for the eggs, but plural: an unspecified number of them, so the plural partitive «des» does the job instead.
Same contraction one more time — «beurre» is masculine too, so it's «du» again, not «un beurre» or bare «beurre».

lines.en: I also read "leeks", I think.
But with that handwriting, it looks like "pears", not "leeks".

notes.note: «on dirait» doesn't literally mean "one would say" — together the two words just mean "it looks like". With this handwriting, «poireaux» looks close enough to «poires» to read as the wrong word entirely.

lines.en: So I didn't buy leeks, but pears.

notes.note: «ai» is the helper carrying the tense, so that's what «ne» and «pas» wrap around, not «acheté». «Je n'ai acheté pas» is never correct.

«poireaux» would normally take «des» — some leeks. Because the verb is negated, the article drops to bare «de». Notice «des poires» right after keeps its full form: nothing is negated there, he really did buy them.

lines.en: Then, I saw "salt", or maybe "honey".
I took the closest jar: it was honey.

notes.note: «j'ai pris» is the event — one action, grabbing a jar. «c'était» is imparfait because it isn't something that happened; it's what turned out to already be true. The jar had been honey the whole time, he just hadn't looked yet.
«le plus proche» is how French builds "the closest" — there's no "-est" ending to add. «plus» goes right in front of the adjective, with «le» agreeing with «pot», which is masculine.

lines.en: Finally, the list said "jam", but I read "mustard".

notes.note: «confiture» is feminine, so unlike «du pain» earlier, «de» and «la» don't contract — they just sit side by side as two separate words, both needed.
Same feminine partitive, same shape, just the wrong jar this time.

lines.en: I came home with a bag full of bad mistakes.

notes.note: «rentrer» is another of the être verbs, like «aller» earlier — coming home counts as the kind of movement that takes «être» instead of «avoir».
«plein» already says the bag is full, so «erreurs» gets bare «de» in front of it instead of a partitive article — the same move as «un peu de» and «beaucoup de» earlier in the story.
«erreurs» is feminine and plural, so the adjective picks up both endings, «-e» for feminine and «-s» for plural, even though you can't hear the difference when you say it.

«mauvais» is one of a small set of common, short adjectives — about size, age, beauty, or goodness — that jump in front of the noun instead of following it like most French adjectives do. That's why it's «mauvaises erreurs», not «erreurs mauvaises».

lines.en: In front of the door, I was afraid of what she was going to say.

notes.note: «j'ai eu peur» is the event — one moment of fear, right there at the door. «allait dire» is imparfait because it isn't something that happened; it's what the narrator expected was still coming, already hanging over the scene before she said a word.
«que» meets «elle», a word starting with a vowel sound, and drops its own vowel the same way «que» does with «il» elsewhere in this story.

lines.en: But when she saw the pears and the honey, my mother laughed really hard.
"It's not a big deal," she said. "We'll make do."

notes.note: Interrupting the sentence with «elle a» to add a dialogue tag would collide two vowel sounds, «a» and «elle». The «t» that slides between them doesn't mean anything — it's only there to make the words sayable together.
Only one verb here, «est» — no helper, no participle — so «ne» and «pas» just close around it directly. It's the plain version of the same sandwich seen earlier with compound tenses.

lines.en: She cut the pears with a bit of cheese.

notes.note: Third time this pattern shows up: «un peu» already names the amount, so «fromage» gets bare «de» in front of it, not a partitive article.

lines.en: With the honey, she made a sauce for the chicken.
We ate that dinner of pears and honey together, laughing.

notes.note: «en» is the one preposition that doesn't take the plain infinitive afterward — it takes this «-ant» form instead. «En riant» means "while laughing", the thing they were doing at the same time as eating.

lines.en: My mother kept the list in her pocket, with a smile.

notes.note: «sa» matches «poche», a feminine word — it doesn't tell you anything about the mother's own gender, even though she happens to be a "she" too. If the pocket were a masculine word, this same sentence would use «son» instead, no matter who owned it.

lines.en: Anyway, every Saturday, it's the same story.

notes.note: «même» sits in front of the noun here, and that position is what gives it the meaning "same" — the story repeats every week. Move it after the noun instead — «l'histoire même» — and it would mean "the story itself", a completely different idea.

stories.title: Le chat du troisième
stories.titleEn: The cat from the third floor
stories.summary: A grey cat has a different name on every floor of the building, and the child who sets out to find its real owner discovers there isn't just one.

lines.en: There's a grey cat in the building.

notes.note: «il», «y», and «a» don't mean it, there, and has on their own here — together the three words just mean there is. It's how the cat gets introduced into the story, the same way you'd start telling someone about him.

lines.en: Nobody knows whose cat he is.

notes.note: Here «personne» (nobody) is the one doing the not-knowing, so it comes first and «ne» follows it, right before the verb. It's the same negative word you'll see later in the story, just moved because this time it's the subject.
«être» plus «à» plus a name is how French says who something belongs to. «à qui est le chat ?» is literally "to whom is the cat" — the everyday way of asking whose cat it is.

lines.en: The cat knows every door in the building.

notes.note: «toutes» agrees with «portes», which is feminine and plural, so it picks up both endings. Later on you'll see «tout le monde», where «tout» stays masculine and singular because it's describing a different, singular idea — everyone, not the doors.
«le» runs into «immeuble», which starts with a vowel sound, so it drops its own vowel and becomes «l'» — the same contraction you'll see with «l'escalier» a couple of lines from here.

lines.en: Every day, he climbs the stairs and picks a door.

notes.note: «le» runs into «escalier», which starts with a vowel sound, so it drops its own vowel and becomes «l'». You'll see the same move happen to «que» a few lines further on.

lines.en: On the first floor, he eats at Monsieur Duval's.

notes.note: «chez» plus a person's name means at that person's home — there's no separate French word for "someone's place" the way English just says "at Duval's." It always needs «chez» in front.

lines.en: There, everyone calls him Gris.

notes.note: «l'» stands for the cat and sits right in front of «appelle», the verb that's actually doing the calling. English puts it after — calls him — but French always moves the pronoun to the left of the verb it belongs to.

«tout» stays masculine and singular here because «tout le monde» — everyone — is a fixed phrase, not a case of agreement changing shape. Compare «toutes les portes» a moment ago, where «toutes» really does agree, feminine and plural, with «portes».

lines.en: On the second floor, he sleeps on the windowsill.
The neighbour on the second floor calls him Moustache.
Léo lives on the third floor, just above.
In the afternoon, the cat sleeps in front of his own window too.

notes.note: «sa fenêtre» already means his window, so adding «à lui» afterwards is pure emphasis — his own, not the neighbours'. That extra «lui» is the standalone pronoun French adds to underline whose something is.
«sa» matches «fenêtre», a feminine word, even though «le chat» is «il», grammatically masculine. The possessive always tracks the thing owned, never the owner.

lines.en: Léo gives him a little milk in an old cup.

notes.note: «lui» stands for the cat and sits right in front of «donne», the verb it belongs to — to him, moved to the left the way object pronouns always are in French.
«un peu» already says how much — a little — so no article follows «de». Compare it to «du lait» with no quantity word at all, which would just mean some milk with no sense of how much.
«vieille» is the feminine form, matching «tasse», a feminine word. Say «vieux tasse» out loud and it clashes — the ending has to change with the noun it's describing.

lines.en: He calls him Cloud, because he's grey like a cloud.

notes.note: «que» meets «il», another word starting with a vowel sound, and contracts the same way «le» did with «escalier» earlier. Say «parce que il» out loud and you'll hear why it can't stay whole.

lines.en: One day, Léo decided to find out whose cat it was.

notes.note: «décider» needs «de» before whatever comes next, and what follows is the plain form of the verb, «trouver», never an "-ing" form. English says decided to find; French just glues «de» and the infinitive straight onto «décidé».
Same construction as earlier in the story — «être» plus «à» plus who something belongs to. Léo isn't hunting for a person called "the owner"; he's trying to find out who the cat is «à».

lines.en: He knocked on every door in the building.

notes.note: «frapper» always comes with «à» attached to it — you don't just knock a door in French, you knock at it. English drops the preposition entirely, but French verbs like this one keep theirs no matter what.

Same agreement as the first time this phrase showed up. «toutes» matches «portes», feminine and plural, so it stays «toutes», not «tous» — the ending doesn't change no matter how many doors he's already tried.

lines.en: "Is this your cat?" he asked each neighbour.

notes.note: Flipping «il a» round to ask a question would give «a-il», two vowels crashing into each other. French slides in a meaningless «t» just to make the question sayable, the same fix you'd see with any «il» or «elle» question in this tense.

lines.en: "No," Monsieur Duval replied, "but I feed him."

notes.note: «lui» stands for the cat and again sits before the verb it belongs to, «donne» — the same leftward move as «l'appelle» earlier in the story. Here it means to him rather than replacing the cat directly the way «l'» did, but the rule about where the pronoun goes doesn't change.

«donner à manger» means "to feed" — literally "to give to eat". «à» here is followed by the plain infinitive «manger», the same pattern as «de trouver» earlier, just with a different preposition glued to a different verb.

lines.en: "No," the neighbour on the second floor replied, "but he sleeps at my place on Saturdays."

notes.note: A bare «samedi» would mean this coming Saturday. Adding «le» turns it into a routine — every Saturday, as a rule — which is exactly what the neighbour means: a regular thing, not a one-off.

lines.en: Finally, Léo understood: the cat doesn't belong to anyone.

notes.note: This time «personne» comes after the verb instead of before it, because it's the thing being denied — the cat belongs to nobody — rather than the one doing the not-knowing, like back in the second line. «ne» still wraps around the verb either way.
«être» plus «à» is how French says something belongs to someone — here it's just negated. «à personne» is "belongs to nobody", the same shape as «c'est à moi» said the ordinary, positive way.

lines.en: Or maybe he belongs to the whole building.

notes.note: «est à» is the same "belongs to" construction as the rest of the story, just aimed at the whole building this time instead of one person.

lines.en: That evening, Léo left his window open.

notes.note: «sa» agrees with «fenêtre», a feminine word, even though the window belongs to Léo, a boy. French possessives track the gender of the thing owned, not the owner — say «son fenêtre» and it would sound wrong before you could explain why.
«ouverte» comes after «fenêtre», which is where most French adjectives sit. It isn't on the short list of common words — like «vieux» or «petit» — that jump in front of the noun instead.
«ouverte» adds an «e» to match «fenêtre», feminine. Léo isn't just leaving the window open in some generic sense — the word itself has to agree with what's open.

lines.en: The grey cat came in, and picked, as always, the best spot.

notes.note: «entrer» is one of the small set of verbs, like «rester» or «arriver», that build their past with «être» instead of «avoir». The cat is a single «il», so the participle stays plain «entré» with no extra letter.

«meilleure» is the irregular superlative of «bon» — it means "best", not "more good". French skips «plus» entirely for this one word and swaps in a different form instead, the way English swaps "good" for "best".

lines.en: He fell asleep on Léo's bed, and nobody came to fetch him.

notes.note: «s'endormir» means to fall asleep, and verbs like this one, where the subject is also the target of the action, always build their past tense with «être», never «avoir». That's why it's «s'est endormi», not «s'a endormi», even though most verbs in this tense use «avoir».

«le» stands for the cat and this time sits in front of «chercher», the infinitive it belongs to, not the conjugated verb «est venu». The pronoun always attaches to the verb it's actually the object of, wherever that verb sits in the sentence.

stories.title: Le vélo jaune
stories.summary: A battered yellow bicycle keeps disappearing and reappearing down the street, and the neighbours' confident theories give way to a far more ordinary explanation.

lines.en: An old yellow bicycle appears in front of the building, one Monday morning.

notes.note: «immeuble» starts with a vowel sound, so «le» can't stay whole in front of it — it drops the «e» and becomes «l'». Say "le immeuble" out loud and you'll hear the clash it avoids.

«vieux» describes age, one of the short, common adjectives that jump in front of the noun instead of following it. «jaune», a colour, stays in its normal spot after the noun, so the bicycle ends up sandwiched between the two.

lines.en: It's an old bicycle, chained to a tree with a chain, but nobody recognizes it.

notes.note: The bicycle just got a new name, «bicyclette», and it's feminine, so «vieux» has to switch to its feminine form «vieille» — same word as the bike in the line above, just wearing the ending that matches its new noun.

«personne» sits before «ne» here because it's the subject of the sentence — nobody is the one not recognizing the bike. The negation still needs both pieces even though «personne» already carries the "no one" idea on its own.
«la» stands for the bicycle — «bicyclette» is feminine, which is why it's «la» and not «le» — and it sits right in front of «reconnaît» instead of after it, the way English would say "recognizes it."

lines.en: On Tuesday morning, it's no longer there.

notes.note: Swap «pas» for «plus» and the sentence stops meaning "isn't there" and starts meaning "isn't there anymore." The bike hasn't just vanished for a moment — it's genuinely gone from that spot now.

lines.en: Someone sees it further down the street, in front of the bakery.

notes.note: «le» stands for the bicycle and sits in front of «voit» — French never says «quelqu'un voit le», it moves the pronoun to the left of the verb every time.

lines.en: The neighbours drink coffee and invent theories.

notes.note: The neighbours aren't drinking one specific, whole coffee — «café» is masculine, so «de» plus «le» contracts to «du», meaning some coffee, an amount with no number attached.
Same idea for the theories: an unspecified number of them, invented on the spot, so the plural partitive «des» carries that sense. English just says theories and leaves the amount implied.

lines.en: Madame Dubois is certain it's a thief's bicycle.

notes.note: Madame Dubois is a woman, so the adjective «certain» takes an «e» to match her: «certaine». She's the first of three confident neighbours in a row, and, like the others, she's wrong.
«de» meets «un», another vowel sound, and contracts the same way «le» did to «l'» in the first line — French won't let two vowel sounds sit next to each other unglued.

lines.en: Monsieur Roux is sure the bicycle moves by itself at night.

notes.note: Nobody is named as the one moving the bicycle — it just «se déplace», moves itself. That's exactly the theory Monsieur Roux is proposing, and the grammar itself sounds a little spooky because of it.
Monsieur Roux is a man, so «sûr» stays in its plain masculine form — no extra letter needed, unlike Madame Dubois's «certaine» just before.

lines.en: The kids are sure it's a magic bicycle.
Every day, the bicycle changes streets, but always with the same broken wheel.

notes.note: «changer de rue» doesn't mean "change of the street" — «de» is glued to «changer» as part of the verb itself, with no article ever following it. Word for word it looks odd; as a fixed pair it just means "switch streets."
«même» in front of the noun means the same wheel, the very thing everyone keeps noticing. Move it after the noun — «la roue même» — and it would mean the wheel itself, a different idea entirely.

lines.en: One day, Madame Dubois decides to attach a note to the handlebar.

notes.note: «de» runs into «attacher», a verb starting with a vowel, and contracts the same way it did before «un» a few lines back. The apostrophe is the only trace left of the missing «e».

lines.en: On the bicycle, there's a note: "Whose bike is this?"

notes.note: None of the three words means anything on its own here — together they just mean "there is." It's how the note gets introduced into the story, tied to the bicycle rather than to any person.

lines.en: For three days, there's no reply.

notes.note: The same fixed phrase as before, now negated: «il n'y a pas» means "there isn't." The three days of silence are what makes the eventual reply land as a surprise.
A plain sentence would say «il y a une réponse». Once it's negated, the article «une» shrinks down to bare «de» — French stops marking the amount once the thing doesn't exist.

lines.en: Then, one morning, someone attached a reply to the handlebar.
Madame Dubois reads it aloud, in front of all the neighbours.

notes.note: «la» stands for the reply, «réponse», which is feminine — that's why it isn't «le» — and it moves in front of «lit» rather than sitting after it, the way English does with "reads it."

lines.en: The reply is simple: "It's my bike."
"I move it every day to make my wife believe I'm exercising."

notes.note: «le» stands for the bicycle again and sits in front of «déplace», the same placement rule as every other object pronoun in this story.
After the preposition «pour», French uses the plain dictionary form of the verb, «faire», not an "-ing" form. English would say "to make her believe," with "to" doing the same job «pour» does here.
«faire du sport» is a fixed block meaning to exercise — literally it reads "make of the sport," which is nonsense assembled word by word. Learn it as one piece, the way you'd learn "faire attention."

lines.en: The neighbours burst out laughing in front of the building.
Madame Dubois went to see the old man to say thank you.

notes.note: «aller» is one of the small set of verbs that build their past with «être» instead of «avoir». Because the subject is Madame Dubois, a woman, the participle picks up an «e»: «allée».
«vieux» would put two vowel sounds back to back in «vieux homme», so French swaps in the special form «vieil» instead — the same move the story's very first line made with «l'immeuble».

lines.en: Since that day, the yellow bicycle always stays in the same spot.

notes.note: «depuis ce jour» marks the day the habit started, and the habit is still going on now — that's what «depuis» signals, unlike «pendant», which would mean the habit was already over and done.

lines.en: Nobody knows his address, but everyone knows his bicycle.

notes.note: «adresse» is feminine, so you'd expect «sa» — but it starts with a vowel, and «sa» becomes «son» there purely for the sound, the same shift the rule describes for words like «amie». It still means his address, not anyone else's.

lines.en: Every morning, he says hello, and his yellow bicycle waits beside him.

notes.note: After a preposition like «à côté de», French needs the standalone pronoun «lui», not a form that glues onto a verb. It's the same slot «elle» fills after «au-dessus de».

stories.title: Sous le même parapluie
stories.summary: A woman shares a stranger's umbrella one rainy morning, and it turns into a small daily habit.

lines.en: Léa lives on a small street, next to a bakery.

notes.note: «de» would run straight into «une», two vowel sounds with nothing between them, so it drops its own vowel and becomes «d'». You'll see the same move happen to «le» and «la» later in the story.

lines.en: Every morning, she buys bread and croissants before work.

notes.note: Léa isn't buying one specific, whole loaf — «pain» is masculine, so «de» plus «le» contracts to «du», and together they mean some bread, an amount with no number attached.
Same idea for the croissants: an unspecified number of them, so the plural partitive «des» does the job. English just says croissants and leaves the amount implied.

lines.en: She waits for the bus in front of the bakery.
There's always a man at the same stop, but she doesn't know his name.

notes.note: Nothing here literally means it, there, or has on its own — the three words work as one fixed phrase for there is. It's how the man at the stop gets introduced into the story.

lines.en: One Tuesday, it had been raining since morning.

notes.note: «depuis» plus this imparfait form, «pleuvait», says the rain had already been going on before this moment and was still happening then — not one downpour, but weather that was already the backdrop.

lines.en: Léa ran to the bus stop.

notes.note: The line before this one set the scene with «pleuvait» — imparfait, ongoing. This verb switches to passé composé because running to the stop is a single, finished action: she started, she arrived, done.
«à l'arrêt» alone would just name where she ended up. «jusqu'à» adds the whole distance she covered getting there — she ran the entire way.

lines.en: She looked for her umbrella in her bag, but it wasn't there.

notes.note: Searching her bag, «a cherché», is the event; the umbrella simply not being there is the state she found. That's why the two verbs sit in different tenses in the same sentence.

Two lines, two different things called «son» — «son parapluie» and now «son sac» — because both «parapluie» and «sac» are masculine words, not because two different people own them. It's always Léa's.

lines.en: She'd left it on the kitchen table.

notes.note: «l'» stands for the umbrella and sits right in front of «a», the helping verb. English puts it after the verb — left it — but French moves it left and keeps it there.

lines.en: The bus wasn't there yet.
The man raised his black umbrella above her.

notes.note: «de» meets «elle», another vowel start, and contracts the same way it did in the first line of the story — this time after the compound preposition «au-dessus», above.
After a preposition like «au-dessus de», French needs the standalone pronoun «elle», not a form that hides in front of a verb. It's the same slot «lui» fills after «sans» or «chez».

lines.en: "You don't have an umbrella?" he asked.

notes.note: Asked as a plain fact, this would be «un parapluie». Once «ne … pas» is in the sentence, the article shrinks to bare «de» — the same drop you'd see in a statement.
Flipping «il a» to make a question would give «a-il», two vowels colliding. French drops in a «t» that carries no meaning at all — it's only there to make the question sayable.

lines.en: "No, I forgot it," Léa replied, and she laughed.

notes.note: «le», standing for the umbrella, meets «ai» and loses its vowel the same way «de» and «que» do elsewhere in the story. Say «le ai» out loud and you'll hear why it can't stay whole.

lines.en: They stayed under the umbrella until the bus arrived.

notes.note: «rester» is one of the small set of verbs that build their past with «être» instead of «avoir». Because the subject is «ils», the participle picks up an «s»: «restés», the way an adjective would.
Same word, same job as the first time it appeared: not just where they end up, but the whole stretch of time they stood there, right up to the bus turning up.

lines.en: On the bus, they talked for the first time.

notes.note: «fois» is feminine, so the ordinal «premier» takes its feminine form, «première», with the extra «e». Say «premier fois» out loud in French and it sounds wrong before you can explain why.

lines.en: She learned his name was Thomas, and that he works near her place.

notes.note: English would happily drop that here: she learned he's called Thomas. French can't; «que» has to introduce what she learned, and it shortens to «qu'» because «il» starts with a vowel.
«chez elle» means at her place, near where she lives — there's no French word that just means home the way English has one, so «chez» plus the person does that job instead.

lines.en: Since that day, Léa never forgets her umbrella.

notes.note: That Tuesday marked a starting point, and the habit is still going now, so it's «depuis», not «pendant». If the habit had already ended, French would switch to «pendant ce jour-là».
«plus» here means not any more, not more — she used to forget it and now she doesn't. Read the sentence with a silent «s» on «plus» and that's the sense you want.

lines.en: She even brings a second one, for Thomas.

notes.note: «en» stands in for parapluies without naming it again — a second one of them. Leave it out and «elle apporte même un deuxième» is missing a piece; French won't let the sentence stand without it.

lines.en: It doesn't always rain, but she brings it anyway.

notes.note: Same empty «il» as the rain earlier in the story — nothing is doing the raining, the pronoun is just a placeholder the sentence needs to have a subject at all.
«pleut» is the only verb in the sentence, so that's what the negation wraps — no helping verb here to argue about, unlike the compound tenses earlier in the story.

lines.en: One morning, Thomas arrives with two coffees.
"For you," he says, "rain or not."
Now, they wait for the bus together, every morning.
And Léa doesn't walk home alone anymore when it rains.

notes.note: The same not any more as before, now about walking home alone rather than forgetting an umbrella — the routine that changed is different, but the grammar doing the work is identical.
«seul» adds an «e» to agree with Léa, who's «elle», not «il». Drop the «e» and the sentence would technically describe a man walking home alone.

stories.title: Le banc du parc
stories.summary: Two strangers share opposite ends of a park bench every day without speaking, until an empty bench makes one of them realize how little she knows about the other.

lines.en: Claire always sits at the same end of the bench, with a book.

notes.note: «asseoir» would mean to sit someone else down. Add «s'» and it turns back on Claire herself — she sits herself down, which is just «to sit» in English.

lines.en: An old man sits at the other end, with a bag of bread.

notes.note: «vieux homme» would crash two vowel sounds together, so French swaps in the special form «vieil» right before a word starting with a vowel or a silent «h».

lines.en: Every morning, he throws pieces of bread to the birds.

notes.note: He isn't throwing one whole loaf, just an unspecified number of pieces — «des» marks that vague amount, the same job it does with croissants or bread elsewhere in these stories.

lines.en: Claire never speaks to him, and he never really looks at her.

notes.note: Swap «pas» for «jamais» and the sentence goes from "doesn't" to "never" — the same wrapping position around the verb, just a different word for the negative.

lines.en: But she always notices his old shoes, worn but clean.

notes.note: «ses» tells you the shoes are plural and says nothing about whether the owner is a man or a woman. Only the story tells you it's the old man's shoes, not Claire's.
«chaussures» is feminine and plural, so the adjective picks up both markers at once: «usée» becomes «usées».

lines.en: He notices that she sometimes laughs alone, while reading.

notes.note: «il» alone would already mean he. Putting «Lui» in front adds emphasis — it's his turn to notice something, after the last two lines were about what Claire sees.
English could drop "that" here: he notices she laughs. French can't — «que» has to introduce what he notices, and it shortens to «qu'» before the vowel in «elle».
After most prepositions French uses the plain infinitive, but «en» is the one exception — it takes this «-ant» form instead. «en lisant» means while reading.

lines.en: One Thursday morning, Claire arrives and sits down as always.
Usually, the man was already there with his birds.

notes.note: This sentence sets the scene: how things usually were, morning after morning. The imparfait paints that backdrop. The next line breaks it with a passé composé, for the one morning that didn't match.

lines.en: But that day, the bench stayed empty next to her.

notes.note: «était» in the line before described the usual picture. This verb is passé composé because it marks the one day the picture changed — an empty bench is the new fact, not the routine.

«rester» is one of the small set of verbs that build their past with «être» instead of «avoir». The subject, «le banc», is masculine and singular, so the participle stays plain «resté», with no extra ending.

lines.en: She waited, but no one came to feed the birds.

notes.note: «personne» is its own negative word, meaning nobody. It doesn't team up with «pas» — the «ne» is enough on its own once «personne» is there.

lines.en: Claire realized she didn't even know his name.

notes.note: Realizing is one sharp moment, so it's passé composé. Not knowing his name was already true before that moment and stays true after — that's why the next verb, «connaissait», switches to imparfait.
The «ne ... pas» pair still wraps the conjugated verb, «connaissait». «même», meaning even, just slides in between «ne» and the verb without breaking the pair apart.

lines.en: She didn't know where he lived, or how to find him.

notes.note: «le» stands for the old man and sits right in front of the verb it belongs to, «retrouver». English puts "him" after "find" — French always puts the pronoun first.

lines.en: For a week, no one fed the birds in his place.

notes.note: A week is a finished stretch of time here — it started and it ended — so French uses «pendant». «depuis» would be wrong; that word is for something still going on.

lines.en: The following Friday, Claire brought bread, just in case.

notes.note: Claire isn't bringing one whole, countable loaf — «pain» is masculine, so «de» plus «le» contracts to «du», marking an unspecified amount of bread.

lines.en: And that morning, the man finally came back, more slowly than before.

notes.note: «revenir» is built on «venir», one of the movement verbs that take «être» instead of «avoir» in the past. The subject «l'homme» is masculine and singular, so the participle needs no extra ending.

lines.en: He sat down, his bag of bread in hand.

notes.note: No verb, no "with" — French just tacks the noun phrase on after a comma to describe how he was sitting. English needs "with his bag in hand"; French needs nothing but the comma.

lines.en: Claire asked him if he was doing okay.

notes.note: «si», meaning if, keeps its vowel almost everywhere — except right before «il» and «ils», where it shortens to «s'». It looks exactly like the «s'» of a reflexive verb but here means something completely different.

lines.en: "I was at the hospital," he said. "My daughter had a baby."

notes.note: Being at the hospital is the state he's explaining, so it's imparfait. The next sentence, «a eu», is passé composé because the birth itself was one event, with a beginning and an end.

lines.en: Claire smiled and gave him a piece of her bread.

notes.note: «lui» stands for the old man and moves in front of the helping verb, «a». English says gave him; French never puts the pronoun after «donné».
Two lines ago «son sac» was the old man's bag. Here «son pain» is Claire's bread — «son» only tells you «pain» is masculine, not who owns it.

lines.en: "Thank you for the bread," he said quietly.

notes.note: Flipping «il a» round for this aside would give «a-il», two vowels colliding. French drops in a «t» with no meaning of its own, just to make the inversion sayable.

lines.en: Now, they talk to each other a little, every morning, each at their own end of the bench.

notes.note: With «ils» as the subject, «se parler» doesn't mean each one talking to himself — it means talking to each other. The same «se» that turns a verb back on one person can also point two people at each other.
«son» here just agrees with «bout», a masculine word, and points back at «chacun» — each one, whether that's Claire or the man. It doesn't pick a gender the way "his" or "her" would in English.

stories.title: Le train de 7h12
stories.summary: A man misses the same train twice in one week, and the second time is deliberate.

lines.en: The old man closed the door without a sound.

notes.note: «vieux homme» would put the «eu» sound straight against the «o» of «homme», which French avoids, so the word changes shape to «vieil». Say it out loud and you can hear why: vieil-homme runs together, vieux-homme stumbles.

You'd expect «a fermé» here, and in speech that's exactly what you'd get. This is written storytelling, so the verb takes its written-only form, «ferma». It means the same thing; it just sounds like a book rather than a conversation.

lines.en: She hadn't heard him leave.

notes.note: This «l'» is «le», meaning him — her husband. «Le avait» is unsayable, so the vowel drops out and the word leans onto the next one.
The two halves close around «avait», leaving «entendu partir» outside on the right. Watch where «pas» lands: after the small verb that carries the tense, not after the verb that carries the meaning.

«avait entendu» is a step further back than the rest of the story. He had already gone; her not-hearing happened before that. French marks that extra step back the same way English does, with «had» plus the participle.

lines.en: Outside, it was still raining.

notes.note: Nothing is doing the raining here. This «il» is a placeholder, the way English says "it's raining" without meaning anything by "it".

lines.en: He walked to the station, his hands in his pockets.

notes.note: «à la gare» on its own would just say where he ended up. «jusqu'à» adds the whole distance — he walked the entire way, no bus, no lift.
English needs "his hands, his pockets" here; French says «les». They're obviously his hands, so marking it would be fussy, and «ses mains dans ses poches» sounds like someone learning the language.

lines.en: The 7:12 train was leaving without him, like every Tuesday.

notes.note: «partait» leaves the departure open — the train pulling out, the thing that happens every Tuesday, the background he's standing in. Compare the last line of the story, where the same train «partit». That one is finished.
After «sans» you can't use the little «le» that hides in front of a verb. The standalone form «lui» is what goes after a preposition, and it's the same word you'd use alone: «Lui ? Jamais.»

lines.en: He'd stopped at the corner for no reason, and that had been enough.

notes.note: Plain «arrêter» means stopping something else — a car, a thief. To come to a halt yourself you stop yourself, so the verb needs its «se»: «s'arrêter». And once that «se» is there the past is built with «être», never «avoir».

lines.en: For forty years he had taken that train every morning.

notes.note: «Pendant» is for a stretch of time that's over and done with. The forty years finished; he's retired now. If he still took the train it would be «depuis quarante ans».

lines.en: He knew the name of every station between his house and Rouen.

notes.note: Knowing the names wasn't an event with a start and a finish — it was simply true of him. States like this take «connaissait», not «connut». «Il connut» would mean he found out, in one moment.
There's no French word for "home" as a place you go to. «chez» plus a person means at or to that person's place, so «chez lui» is his house, his flat, wherever he lives.

lines.en: Now there was no office, no colleagues, nobody waiting for him.

notes.note: «pas» isn't the only word that finishes a negation. «plus» in this position means not any more — the office existed once and doesn't now. Read it aloud with a silent «s»; that's usually what tells it apart from «plus» meaning more.
You'd expect «un bureau». After a negation the article collapses to a bare «de», so «un bureau» becomes «plus de bureau» — the same thing happens to «des collègues» right after it.
English puts "-ing" after the preposition: nobody waiting. French can't do that, so «pour» is followed by the plain «attendre», with the «l'» meaning him tucked in front of it.

lines.en: But on Tuesdays he set out all the same.

notes.note: «mardi» on its own would mean one particular Tuesday. Adding «le» turns it into every Tuesday, the standing arrangement — which is the whole point of this sentence.

lines.en: He'd have a coffee across from his old office, walk for an hour, then come home.

notes.note: Three verbs in a row, all in the same form, because none of them is a single event. This is what he did every Tuesday, the shape of the day rather than one particular day. English reaches for "he'd" to say the same thing.
In front of the noun, «ancien» means former — the office he used to work in. Put it after and «un bureau ancien» would be a piece of antique furniture, which is a very different sentence.

lines.en: His wife had never asked him any questions.

notes.note: «lui» here means to him, and it sits in front of the verb group where English puts it after: asked him. Once you have a pronoun instead of a full name, it moves left and stays there.

lines.en: That morning he came home at eleven, his shoes soaked.

notes.note: Everything before this line was the routine. This one verb changes form, and that alone tells you the routine broke — one particular morning, one specific arrival, eleven o'clock instead of the evening.
French can hang a bare noun phrase on the end of a sentence to describe the state someone is in, with no verb and no "with". It's the same move as «les mains dans les poches» in the fourth line.

lines.en: His wife looked up from her paper.

notes.note: «ses yeux» would be odd here — whose eyes could they be? French leaves the ownership implied and uses «les», exactly as it did with his hands and his pockets.

lines.en: He told her he'd missed the train.

notes.note: English lets you drop "that" — he told her he'd missed it. French never does; «qu'» has to be there. And since «il» starts with a vowel, «que» loses its own vowel and becomes «qu'».

lines.en: She didn't ask him which one.

notes.note: "Which one" is a single word in French, and it carries the gender and number of what it stands for. It's standing in for «le train» here, so it comes out masculine and singular: «lequel».

lines.en: The following Friday he got up before the alarm.

notes.note: «lever» is to lift something. What he lifts is himself, so the «se» is doing real work: «se lever» is how French says get up. Drop it and you've said he lifted something, and the sentence stops making sense.

lines.en: It had stopped raining.
He got to the station ten minutes early.

notes.note: «arriver» takes «à» before a place, always — you can't arrive a station in French any more than you can in English. The «à» is part of the verb's habit, not something you choose.

lines.en: The train was already there, doors open.

notes.note: «ouvert» grows an «e» for the feminine «portes» and an «s» because there are several — «ouvertes». You can't hear the difference when it's read aloud, but leaving it off looks wrong on the page.

lines.en: He sat down on a bench, his ticket in his hand.

notes.note: «son» doesn't tell you the owner is male — it tells you «billet» is a masculine word. His wife's ticket would also be «son billet» — and «son journal», seven lines back, was hers for exactly the same reason.

lines.en: A woman asked him if he was getting on.

notes.note: «si» meaning if normally keeps its vowel — «si elle montait» is fine. In front of «il» and «ils» only, it shortens to «s'», which is why this looks like the «s'» of a reflexive verb but isn't one.

lines.en: He shook his head.

notes.note: French says he made no with the head. There's no verb for shaking your head; «faire» plus «oui» or «non» covers both, and it's the ordinary everyday way to say it.

lines.en: The doors closed.

notes.note: Nobody is closing them, and «les portes fermèrent» would be wrong. The «se» is how French says a thing happens to itself when the doer is irrelevant — here, the doors close on their own schedule, which is rather the point.

lines.en: The 7:12 train left without him.

notes.note: Same train, same words, one letter of difference from the fifth line of the story. «partait» was a train in the act of leaving, every Tuesday. «partit» is one departure, complete, and he watched it happen.

lines.en: He walked home through the back streets, taking his time.

notes.note: English would say "without hurrying". French puts the plain infinitive after «sans», and «se presser» keeps its «se» because what he isn't hurrying is himself.

lines.en: His wife was standing in the kitchen, and there were two cups on the table.

notes.note: Word for word this is "it there had", which is no help at all. Taken together the three words mean there was or there were — and unlike English, the phrase never changes for a plural. Two cups, still «il y avait».

lines.en: She'd been setting out two since Tuesday.

notes.note: «en» stands in for «des tasses» — of them. French won't let you say «elle mettait deux» and stop there; if you don't name the thing, «en» has to hold its place in front of the verb.
«depuis» plus this form of the verb is how French says something started back then and is still going. English needs a whole scaffolding — she'd been setting out — where French needs one preposition.

stories.title: Les clés du voisin
stories.summary: A narrator finds a stranger's keys on the stairs, spends a week trying to return them, and finally meets the neighbour they had already crossed paths with many times without knowing their name.

lines.en: One Monday morning, it was still cold, and the stairway of my building was empty.

notes.note: «il» doesn't stand for a person or a thing here — French just needs a subject for weather, the same empty «il» you'd see in «il pleut», it's raining. Nothing is actually cold in a way «il» could point to.
«le» would run straight into «escalier», a word starting with a vowel sound, so it drops its own vowel and becomes «l'». You'll see the same move happen to «de» later in the story.

lines.en: I found a keyring on a step, all alone.
There were two keys on it, a big one and a small one.

notes.note: «il», «y», and «avait» only mean something as one block: there was. It's how the keys get introduced into the story, the same way «il y a» would do it in the present.
«clé» is feminine, so both size words end in «e» to match it — «grand» and «petit» would be the versions for a masculine noun. You can't hear the difference out loud, but it has to be written.

lines.en: They weren't mine.

notes.note: French doesn't have a separate verb for belonging — «être» plus «à» plus a person does the job. «Elles sont à moi» would mean they're mine; the negation here just flips it around.
Only one verb here, «étaient», so «ne» and «pas» simply close around it — no helping verb to complicate things yet, unlike the compound tenses coming up soon.

lines.en: I told myself that someone had lost their keys.

notes.note: «se dire» means to tell yourself something — «me» shows the telling loops back to the narrator. Reflexive verbs like this always build the passé composé with «être», never «avoir», which is why it's «suis», not «ai».
English could drop that here — I told myself someone lost their keys — but French can't. «que» has to introduce what was said, even inside your own head.

lines.en: I wanted to know whose keys these were.

notes.note: Asking whose something is uses the same «être à» pattern as saying it plainly, just turned into a question. «à qui» stands where «à moi» or «à elle» would go, asking which person the «à» points to.

lines.en: On the first floor, I knocked on an old man's door.

notes.note: «vieux» would put two vowel sounds back to back in «vieux homme» — the «h» is silent, so it's really «vieux + omme». French swaps in the special form «vieil» to avoid that collision.

lines.en: They weren't his keys either.
On the second floor, a lady told me these keys weren't hers.

notes.note: Same rule as before: what she said has to be introduced with «que», even though English would happily just say a lady told me these keys weren't hers.
Same shape as «à moi» a few lines back, just with «elle» instead — the standalone pronoun that has to follow a preposition like «à».

lines.en: On the third floor, I knocked, but nobody answered.

notes.note: «personne» takes the place of «pas» here and means nobody — it's the subject of the sentence, not something sitting after the verb the way it does in «il n'y a personne». It still pairs with «ne» the same way «plus» and «jamais» do.

lines.en: I went down to the bakery, at the bottom of the building.

notes.note: «descendre» is one of the small set of movement verbs that build the passé composé with «être» instead of «avoir» — the same family as «aller» and «rentrer». That's why it's «je suis descendu», never «j'ai descendu».

lines.en: I showed the keys to the baker, but he didn't know them.

notes.note: «j'ai montré» is the event — one action, holding the keys out. «il ne connaissait pas» is imparfait because not recognising them isn't something that happened; it's the state the baker was already in.

lines.en: So, I wrote a note and stuck it up near the mailboxes.

notes.note: «l'» stands for the note and sits right in front of «ai», the helper verb. English says stuck it up after the verb; French moves the pronoun left and keeps it there.

lines.en: The note said: "I found some keys. They aren't mine. Maybe they're yours?"

notes.note: «clés» is plural, so «des» does the job «du» or «de la» would do for something singular — an unspecified number of keys, not a count.

Both halves of the note lean on the same «être à» pattern the narrator used out loud earlier — «à moi» rules the keys out as the narrator's, and «à vous» asks whoever reads the note if they're theirs.

lines.en: I left my phone number at the bottom of the page.
A neighbour read my note, and told me: "That's kind of you."
On Tuesday, nobody phoned.
On Wednesday, I asked the caretaker, but she didn't know anything.

notes.note: «j'ai demandé» is the one-off event, going and asking. «elle ne savait rien» is imparfait because not knowing isn't an action — it's a state she was already in before the narrator even asked.

lines.en: I left the keys on the kitchen table.
Every evening, coming home, I saw them on the table.

notes.note: «en» is the one preposition that doesn't take the plain infinitive after it — it takes this «-ant» form instead. «En rentrant» means while coming home, something happening at the same time as noticing the keys.
«les» stands for the keys and sits in front of «voyais» rather than after it — the same leftward move object pronouns always make.

lines.en: The keys weren't just keys any more.

notes.note: «plus» here doesn't mean more — paired with «ne», it means not any more. The keys used to be just keys, and that had stopped being true.

lines.en: They became a small weight on the table.

notes.note: «devenir» is another être verb, like «descendre» earlier — and because the subject is «elles», the keys, the participle picks up an «s», «devenues», agreeing the way an adjective would.

lines.en: Thursday, I put a cup of coffee next to the keys, but nobody came.

notes.note: «personne» is the subject again, nobody, and «venir» is one of the être verbs — so together it's «personne n'est venu». «venu» stays in its plain masculine form because «personne» is always treated as masculine, whoever it turns out to mean.

lines.en: Friday, my mail and a book were around them too.

notes.note: «de» meets «elles», a vowel start, and drops its own vowel the same way it did with «l'escalier» right at the start of the story.
After a preposition like «autour de», French needs this standalone «elles», not a form that hides in front of a verb — the same slot «moi» and «elle» filled after «à» earlier on.

lines.en: Because of the keys, my kitchen table was full of little things.

notes.note: «table» is feminine, so «plein» picks up an «e» to match it, «pleine». Say «ma table était plein» out loud and it's immediately wrong, even though you can't hear the missing letter.
«petit» is one of a short list of common adjectives — about size, age, beauty, or goodness — that jump in front of the noun instead of following it, unlike most French adjectives.

lines.en: In the evening, before sleeping, I still thought about the keys.

notes.note: Where English puts an -ing form after before — before sleeping — French uses the plain dictionary form of the verb instead: «avant de dormir», never «avant de dormant».

lines.en: The keys had been on my table for a week.

notes.note: The keys didn't sit there for a week and then stop — they were still there, so French uses «depuis» with the imparfait rather than «pendant», which would mark a stretch that's already over.

lines.en: I still had no answer to my note.

notes.note: «réponse» would normally take «une» in front of it, an answer. Once the sentence is negative, there isn't one at all, so the article shrinks to bare «de».

lines.en: I thought nobody was going to come.

notes.note: «personne» is the subject again — nobody was going to come — paired with «ne» the same way as before. This time it wraps around «allait», the conjugated piece of «allait venir», while «venir» itself sits untouched right after it.
«que» has to introduce the thought here too — French never drops it the way English drops that in I thought nobody was going to come.

lines.en: The following Friday, someone knocked at my door.
I opened the door.
It was the woman from the bakery.

notes.note: «j'ai ouvert» just before this is the event, one action, opening the door. «c'était» is imparfait because it isn't something that happened — it's simply who turned out to already be standing there.

lines.en: I saw her almost every morning, but I didn't know her name.

notes.note: «la» stands for the woman and sits in front of «voyais», the same leftward move «les» made earlier when it stood for the keys.

«son» agrees with «nom», a masculine word — it says nothing about the woman herself, even though «son» looks like it should mean his. If the word for name were feminine, this same sentence about this same woman would use «sa» instead.

lines.en: She always bought the same thing, a coffee and a croissant.
"Excuse me," she said. "I think these are my keys."

notes.note: Dropping in a dialogue tag with «elle a» would collide two vowel sounds, «a» and «elle». The «t» that slides between them doesn't mean anything on its own — it's only there to make the words sayable together.
«que» is required here too — French can't just say I think these are my keys without it, the way English sometimes drops that.

lines.en: "I've looked for these keys everywhere," she explained.
I gave her the keys right away.

notes.note: «lui» stands for the woman, to her, and sits in front of «ai» instead of after «donné» the way English puts it. It works whether the person is male or female; only the sentence tells you which.

lines.en: She thanked me, and then she smiled.
She told me her name was Camille.

notes.note: «que» is doing the same job again, introducing what she said, and shortens to «qu'» because «elle» starts with a vowel.

«s'appeler» is how French says to be called — literally to call yourself. It stays in the present here even though everything around it is passé composé, because her name being Camille isn't a one-off event; it's a fact that's still true.

lines.en: I told her my name too.

notes.note: «Moi» standing alone at the front adds emphasis, as for me — something «je» alone couldn't do. It's the standalone form French uses whenever a pronoun needs to carry weight on its own, not glued to a verb.

lines.en: We laughed, because we had been living in the same building for a long time.

notes.note: «habitions» is imparfait because living in the same building wasn't a single event — paired with «depuis longtemps» at the end of the sentence, it says the living-there had already been true for a while by the time they met, exactly the kind of ongoing fact «depuis» pairs with.

lines.en: Since that day, Camille and I have coffee together on Saturdays.

notes.note: This time «depuis» pairs with the present tense, «prenons» at the end of the sentence, because the coffee habit hasn't stopped — it's still going as the narrator tells the story. Compare «depuis longtemps» a moment ago, which used the imparfait for a fact about the past instead.

A bare «samedi» would mean one particular Saturday. Adding «le» turns it into a routine, every Saturday, the same trick that turned «vendredi» into a habit here after a whole week of specific, one-off days earlier in the story.

lines.en: On my table, there are no more keys — just two empty cups.

notes.note: «il y a», here negated to «il n'y a plus», is the same fixed block from earlier in the story, now saying there's nothing left instead of announcing what's there.
«tasses» is feminine and plural, so «vide» picks up an «s» for the plural — it already ends in «e», so no separate feminine ending is needed on top of it.

stories.title: Le dernier bus
stories.summary: A woman misses the last bus home and waits anyway, and the strangers who join her make the long walk back better than the ride would have been.

lines.en: Camille works in a restaurant, in town.
That evening, she finished very late, after midnight.
She ran to the stop, but the bus had already left.

notes.note: «à» alone would just say where she ended up. «jusqu'à» adds the whole distance she covered getting there — she ran the entire way.
The bus leaving happened before Camille got to the stop — a past inside the past — so French reaches one step further back than the passé composé: «était parti», not «est parti».

lines.en: The last bus of the night doesn't come back before tomorrow.

notes.note: «repasse» is the only verb in this sentence, so «ne» and «pas» just wrap it directly — the same plain pattern as «je ne mange pas».

lines.en: Camille doesn't have money for a taxi.

notes.note: Said as a plain fact this would be «de l'argent». Once «ne ... pas» lands in the sentence, the amount stops being named at all and the article shrinks to bare «d'».

lines.en: So she decides to wait, even without a reason.
She sat down on the bench at the stop.

notes.note: «s'asseoir» is reflexive, and reflexive verbs always build their past with «être». Camille is «elle», so the participle picks up an «e»: «assise», the way an adjective would.

lines.en: It was cold, but the sky was clear.

notes.note: English says "it was cold" with "to be". French reaches for «faire» instead — nobody makes the cold happen, but the weather still takes this verb, not «être».

lines.en: She looked up and saw some stars.

notes.note: They're obviously her own eyes, so French skips «ses» and uses the plain «les» instead. Adding a possessive here would sound like a learner overexplaining.
Not one specific star — an unnamed number of them — so the plural partitive «des» marks that. English just says "stars" and leaves the amount unsaid.

lines.en: A young man arrived with a big backpack.

notes.note: «jeune» is one of the short, common adjectives — about age, like «vieux» — that jump in front of the noun instead of following it.
Same rule, different noun: «grand» is about size, another word on that short list, so it sits before «sac à dos» too.

lines.en: "Has the bus gone by?" he asked.

notes.note: Flipping «il a» to ask a question would give «a-il», two vowels running straight into each other. French drops in a «t» that means nothing on its own — it only exists to make the question sayable.

lines.en: "Yes, ten minutes ago," Camille replied.

notes.note: The same three words that usually mean "there is" can give a time instead: «il y a dix minutes» is "ten minutes ago", the same way «il y a trois ans» means "three years ago".

lines.en: His name is Léo, and he's coming back from the library.

notes.note: Word for word, «il s'appelle Léo» is "he calls himself Léo" — French always uses the reflexive here, where English just says "his name is".

lines.en: He sat down next to Camille.

notes.note: Same reflexive verb as Camille's, but Léo is «il», not «elle», so the participle stays in its plain form: «assis», no extra «e».

lines.en: They wait together, without talking.

notes.note: English would say "without talking", an -ing form. After a preposition like «sans», French always uses the plain dictionary form of the verb instead: «parler».

lines.en: Ten minutes go by, but the bus still doesn't come.

notes.note: One more plain example: «arrive» is the only verb, so «ne» and «pas» close around it directly, with «toujours» sitting inside the sandwich.

lines.en: A man arrived with a guitar on his back.

notes.note: It's obviously his own back, so French uses the plain «le», not «son». The same move you saw with «les yeux» a moment ago works for any body part.

lines.en: He put his guitar against the bench and sat down.

notes.note: «sa» agrees with «guitare», a feminine word — not with the man who owns it. A woman with the same guitar would also say «sa guitare».

lines.en: "There's no more bus tonight, I think," he said.

notes.note: Swap «pas» for «plus» in the middle of «il y a» and the meaning shifts from "there isn't" to "there isn't anymore" — the bus existed earlier tonight, and now it doesn't.
Once the sentence is negative, «un bus» can't stay whole — the article shrinks to bare «de», the same drop you saw with «d'argent» earlier.

lines.en: His name is Karim, and he plays guitar, right nearby.
Karim has a paper bag, with bread inside.

notes.note: Not a whole, specific loaf — an amount with no number attached, so the partitive «du» carries that sense here, the same as the bread in another story.

lines.en: "Are you hungry?" he asks Camille and Léo.

notes.note: English uses "to be" for hunger. French uses «avoir» — literally "to have" — plus the bare noun «faim», with no article at all.

lines.en: They share the bread, sitting on the bench.

notes.note: No verb, no "while" — French just tacks the state on after a comma. English needs something like "sitting" to do the same job.

lines.en: A woman arrived, very tired.

notes.note: «une femme» is feminine, so the adjective takes the extra «e» — not «fatigué», which would describe a man.

lines.en: Her name is Nadia, and she works at the hospital, at night.

notes.note: A bare time word names one occasion; add «la» and it becomes a routine — the same trick as «le soir» for every evening. Here it means she works nights as a rule.

lines.en: She finished work twenty minutes ago.
"Are you waiting for the bus too?" asks Nadia.
"Me too, I missed it," replies Léo.

notes.note: «je» can only stand glued to a verb. Standing alone for emphasis, at the front of the sentence, needs the strong form instead: «moi».
«l'» stands for the bus and sits in front of «ai», the helping verb. English puts it after the verb — missed it — but French moves it left and keeps it there.

lines.en: Camille smiles, and now there are four of them waiting.
Time passes, but the bus still doesn't come.
Karim picks up his guitar and plays a little song.

notes.note: Another of the short, common adjectives — about size — that goes before the noun instead of after it: «une petite chanson», never «une chanson petite».

lines.en: Nadia closes her eyes for a minute, then she laughs.
"It's like a concert!" says Camille.
They look at the time.
It's half past midnight, and the bus still isn't there.

notes.note: «il» here doesn't stand for anyone — it's just the placeholder French sentences need to have a subject, the same empty «il» that shows up for weather.

lines.en: "I think it's not going to come anymore," says Nadia.

notes.note: English can drop "that" here — I think it's not coming. French can't; «que» has to introduce what she thinks, and it shortens to «qu'» before the vowel in «il».
«va» is the conjugated piece; «venir» is the plain infinitive after it. The negation wraps «va» and leaves «venir» outside, the same split you'd see with a helping verb in the passé composé.

lines.en: So they decide to walk back, all together.
They walk together through the empty streets of the town.

notes.note: «rues» is feminine and plural, so «vide» — already ending in «e» — only needs the extra «s»: «vides».

lines.en: Karim plays guitar while walking.

notes.note: «en» is the one preposition that breaks the infinitive rule — it takes the «-ant» form instead: «en marchant», while walking.

lines.en: Nadia sings a little, even though she's tired.
Nobody complains, even after an hour of walking.

notes.note: «personne» is the subject here, so it sits at the front, before «ne». The pair still needs «ne», but there's no «pas» — «personne» already carries the negative on its own, the same way «plus» and «jamais» do elsewhere in this story.

lines.en: They arrive at Camille's place first.

notes.note: «chez» has no real English equivalent — it means at the home of the person named after it. You can't say «chez la maison»; for a plain building you'd use «à» instead.

lines.en: The others carry on, laughing.
Camille watches her friends leave, then she smiles.

notes.note: «ses» marks a plural owned thing, not a plural owner — it stays «ses» whether the friends are men, women, or both, because «amis» is plural.

lines.en: That last bus never came, and nobody regrets it.

notes.note: «jamais» swaps in for «pas» one more time, and the meaning becomes "never" — the bus didn't just fail to come once tonight, it never came at all.

«le» stands for the bus and moves to the front of the verb group, right between «ne» and «regrette». English leaves the object after the verb — regrets it — but French always tucks the pronoun in before.

stories.title: Le marché du mardi
stories.summary: A teenager helps their grandmother at her vegetable stall on market day, and slowly realises the stall was never really about vegetables.

lines.en: This Tuesday morning, it's still dark when Mamie wakes me up.

notes.note: Nothing is actually "making" the night — «il» is just a placeholder subject French sentences need even when nobody is doing anything, the same empty «il» you get with «il pleut» or «il est sept heures».

lines.en: "Up you get," she says, "I need you at the market."

notes.note: «avoir besoin de» is glued together as one unit meaning "to need." The «de» isn't "of" here and nothing can slide between «besoin» and «de» — treat the whole phrase as one block.

lines.en: I don't feel like getting up, but I follow her down the stairs.

notes.note: «lever» means to lift something; «se lever» means to get yourself up out of bed. The «me» shows the action lands back on the subject — you lift yourself.
«la» stands for Mamie and sits right before «suis», the verb it belongs to. Careful: this is «suivre», to follow — not «être», to be — so «je la suis» means "I follow her," not "I am her."

lines.en: Outside, it's very cold, and my hands are already frozen.

notes.note: French reaches for «faire» — literally "to make" — for weather, where English uses "to be." «il fait froid» is a fixed block; nobody translates «fait» on its own here.
«gelées» picks up an «e» and an «s» to match «mains», which is feminine and plural. You can't hear the difference when you say it, but it has to be there in writing.

lines.en: In the square, Mamie sets up her table: carrots, leeks, potatoes.

notes.note: «sa» agrees with «table», a feminine word — not with Mamie, even though the table is obviously hers either way. French possessives always track the gender of the thing owned.

lines.en: She's come here every Tuesday for forty years, even when it rains.

notes.note: A bare «mardi» would mean one particular Tuesday. Adding «le» turns it into a routine — every Tuesday, as a rule — which is exactly the habit this line is describing.
The habit started forty years ago and is still going now, so French uses «depuis», not «pendant». If it had already stopped, the sentence would need «pendant» instead.

lines.en: "Help me get the tomatoes out," she says, and I understand why I'm here.

notes.note: Object pronouns almost always go before the verb, but a positive command is the one exception — the pronoun jumps after and attaches with a hyphen: «aide-moi», not «me aide».

lines.en: The first customer arrives very early, before everyone else.
It's Monsieur Blanchard; Mamie always gives him the same leeks.

notes.note: «lui» stands for Monsieur Blanchard — to him — and sits in front of «donne», the verb it belongs to. English leaves "him" after the verb; French moves it to the left and keeps it there.

lines.en: "And your wife, is she doing better?" Mamie asks.
"A little better, thank you," he replies, and he picks three more leeks.
I look at the price on the little sign and count the coins.

notes.note: «petit» is one of the short, common adjectives — like «beau» or «grand» — that go in front of the noun instead of after it. Most French adjectives follow the noun; this small group doesn't.

lines.en: The next customer is Madame Vidal, who always buys the same vegetables.

notes.note: «même» itself doesn't change for gender, but it still has to agree in number: an «s» for the plural «légumes», the same way any other adjective would pick up an ending.

lines.en: "The usual?" Mamie asks, without even writing down the order.

notes.note: After «sans», French uses the plain dictionary form of the verb, «écrire», never an "-ing" form. «même» slots in between but doesn't change that — the infinitive still follows the preposition directly.

lines.en: Mamie doesn't need to ask: she already knows what she needs.

notes.note: Same fixed pair as before — «avoir besoin de» — now with an infinitive after it instead of a person. The «de» stays glued on regardless of what follows.

«il faut» is another job for the empty «il»: nothing "needs" anything on its own, the pronoun just fills the subject slot so the sentence has one. «ce qu'il faut» is literally "what it needs" — what's necessary.

lines.en: I start to understand that Mamie doesn't only sell vegetables.

notes.note: English can drop "that" here — "I understand Mamie doesn't only sell..." — but French can't. «que» has to introduce what I'm coming to understand.

lines.en: A young woman arrives with a baby crying in her arms.

notes.note: With parts of the body, French uses the plain «les» instead of a possessive like «ses». Whose arms they are is obvious from context, so saying "her arms" out loud would sound heavy.

lines.en: She counts her coins, but there isn't enough money for the tomatoes.

notes.note: «il y a» is one fixed block meaning "there is." The negation slides its «n'» in between «il» and «y», which looks like it breaks the phrase apart, but the three words are still doing their usual job together.
«assez» already says how much — enough — so no article follows «de». Compare «de l'argent» with no quantity word, which would just mean some money with no amount implied.

lines.en: Mamie puts the tomatoes in the bag anyway, without saying anything.

notes.note: «sans» is followed by the plain form of the verb, «dire», the same pattern as «sans même écrire» earlier. «rien» sits between them but the infinitive still comes right after the preposition.

lines.en: "How much do I owe you?" the young woman asks, a little embarrassed.

notes.note: French can tack a bare description onto the end of a sentence after a comma, describing the state of the person just mentioned — no "and she was" needed, the way English would add it.

lines.en: "Just the carrots, one euro," Mamie replies with a smile.
The young woman says thank you twice and leaves again with a smile.
I ask Mamie why she did that.
"She has three children and no husband," Mamie says.

notes.note: A husband she had would be «un mari». Once the sentence is negated, the article shrinks down to bare «de» — the same drop you'd see with «du» or «des».

lines.en: "The tomatoes cost almost nothing."

notes.note: Swap «pas» for «rien» and the sentence denies not "not doing something" but a thing itself — here, any real cost. «presque» sits inside the pair without breaking it.

lines.en: I look at Mamie, standing in the cold, and I don't say anything more.

notes.note: Another bare tag after a comma, like «un peu gênée» earlier — no verb, just a description of how Mamie is standing there, tacked straight onto the sentence.

«plus» here means not any more, not more of it — I used to say something, now I don't. It stacks with «rien» at the end for "nothing more," but the pair doing the actual negating is still «ne ... plus».

lines.en: An old man approaches slowly, with a cane.

notes.note: «vieux» has a special form just for this spot — right before a masculine noun starting with a vowel sound. «vieil homme» is easier to say than «vieux homme» would be.
«approcher» can mean to bring something closer; «s'approcher» means to come closer yourself. The «s'» sends the action back onto the subject, the old man himself.

lines.en: "Hello Monsieur Roux, the same as usual?" Mamie asks.

notes.note: «de» runs into «habitude», which starts with a vowel sound even though the letter is an "h" — French "h" is silent — so it drops its own vowel and becomes «d'».

lines.en: "Yes, but just for me now," he replies sadly.

notes.note: After a preposition like «pour», French needs the standalone pronoun «moi», not a form that hides in front of a verb. The little pronouns like «me» can't stand alone like this.

lines.en: His son has moved away to live in Lyon, and the house is very quiet.

notes.note: «partir» is one of the verbs that build their past with «être», not «avoir». The subject here, «fils», is a single masculine noun, so the participle stays plain «parti» with no extra letter added.
Cities always take «à» — you don't just go "to Lyon" in French, you go «à» Lyon, and the preposition can't be dropped the way it sometimes can in English.

lines.en: Mamie adds an apple to his bag, without asking him for one more euro.

notes.note: «lui» stands for Monsieur Roux — to him — and sits in front of «demander», the verb it belongs to, even though that verb is an infinitive here rather than a conjugated form.

lines.en: Monsieur Roux says nothing, but he smiles a little before leaving.

notes.note: «avant de» always takes the plain form of the verb after it, «partir» — never an "-ing" form the way English would say "before leaving."

lines.en: By midday, I'm not cold anymore, but the wind still blows.

notes.note: French uses «avoir» — literally "to have" — for how your body feels, where English uses "to be." «avoir froid» is a fixed pair; there's no article and you don't translate «ai» as "have" on its own.

lines.en: I weigh a kilo of carrots and give the change back without a mistake.

notes.note: «kilo» already names the amount, so no «du» or «des» follows «de» — just the bare word, the same pattern as «assez de» or «un peu de».
«tromper» means to deceive someone else; «se tromper» means to be wrong yourself, to make a mistake. The «me» turns the action back onto the person doing it.

lines.en: A woman with white hair stops in front of the table and looks at Mamie.

notes.note: French describes hair the same way it handles other body parts — the plain article «les» (contracted here into «aux», à plus les) instead of a possessive. There's no need to say "her" hair; it's already clear whose it is.

lines.en: "You don't know me?" she asks softly.

notes.note: The negation wraps around the whole verb group, and the object pronoun «me» rides along inside it, tucked between «ne» and the verb rather than sitting outside the pair.

lines.en: "Of course," Mamie replies, and she takes her hands.

notes.note: «lui» already says whose hands they are — the woman's — so «les mains» stays with the plain article instead of a possessive. Adding «ses» on top of «lui» would say the same thing twice.

lines.en: "Thank you again, for last winter," the woman says, her eyes wet.

notes.note: A third bare tag in this story: no verb, just «les yeux mouillés» dropped in after a comma to describe her, the way «debout dans le froid» described Mamie earlier.

lines.en: I don't understand; I've never heard this story.

notes.note: «jamais» swaps in for «pas» to mean never instead of simply not. «n'» still comes right before the verb group; «jamais» lands after it, the same shape as «ne ... pas» or «ne ... plus».

lines.en: The woman leaves, and I ask Mamie: "What winter?"
Mamie hesitates, then she tells the story: her husband was in the hospital for two months.

notes.note: This time the stretch is over — the two months in hospital ended long ago — so French switches to «pendant» instead of the «depuis» from earlier in the story, which was about a habit still going on.

The rest of this scene sits in the present, but the story inside it drops into the imparfait. «était» paints the background fact — he was in hospital — the state the rest of the memory happened inside.

lines.en: Every evening, after the market, Mamie brought her hot soup.

notes.note: «soupe» is feminine, so "some soup" needs «de la», not «du». English can just say "soup"; French always marks that it's an unnamed amount of it.
This isn't one delivery — it's every evening, all winter, so French reaches for the imparfait to paint a repeated habit rather than a single finished event.

lines.en: She had never told me that, not even once.

notes.note: This goes one step further back than the passé composé: «avait» plus the participle means "had done," describing something already true before this whole conversation started.

lines.en: I look at these vegetables on the table, and I don't see them the same way anymore.

notes.note: Same not any more as before — I used to see the vegetables one way, and now, knowing about the soup, I don't. The pair «ne ... plus» wraps around «les vois», with the pronoun riding along inside it.

lines.en: "Are you coming back next Tuesday?" Mamie asks, and she puts away the last leeks.

notes.note: No «le» this time, because Mamie means one specific Tuesday coming up — not the weekly habit from the start of the story. Compare «le mardi» back then, which meant every Tuesday, as a rule.

lines.en: "Yes, Mamie," I answer, and this time, it's true.

rules.name: Verbs that need «à» before a place
rules.body:
Some French verbs come with a preposition attached, and you can't drop it even
when English has none. «arriver» is one: you always arrive **at**.

- Il arriva **à** la gare. — He reached the station.
- Elle est entrée **dans** la cuisine. — She entered the kitchen.
- Nous allons **à** Rouen. — We're going to Rouen.

Cities take «à», feminine countries take «en» (en France), masculine ones take
«au» (au Portugal).

rules.name: Adjectives match the noun in gender and number
rules.body:
An adjective takes an «e» for a feminine noun and an «s» for a plural, in
whatever order applies. You often can't hear it; you always have to write it.

- portes **ouvertes** — feminine and plural, so «-es».
- les chaussures **trempées** — same, and the participle behaves like an adjective.
- un banc **vert**, une porte **verte**, des portes **vertes**.

Adjectives already ending in «e» add only the «s»: «une rue calme», «des rues
calmes».

rules.name: Adjectives that change shape before a vowel
rules.body:
Three common adjectives have a third form used only in front of a masculine
noun starting with a vowel or a silent «h». It exists purely so the words don't
collide when you say them.

- vieux → **vieil** : un vieil homme, un vieil ami. But un vieux monsieur.
- beau → **bel** : un bel été. But un beau jardin.
- nouveau → **nouvel** : un nouvel appartement. But un nouveau bureau.

The feminine forms already end in a consonant sound — vieille, belle, nouvelle —
